triage.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
triage.reason: Sudden painful red eye with halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil; classic emergency presentation reachable by history, exam and tonometry.

demographics: More common in people of East Asian and Southeast Asian descent
More common in women than men
Rare before age 40 unless there is an underlying ocular or systemic trigger

risk_factors.text: East Asian or Southeast Asian ancestry
Shallow anterior chamber or narrow iridocorneal angle on prior eye exam
Recent dilation of the pupils for an eye exam

family_history: Angle-closure glaucoma in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: My eye hurts so much I can't stand it
My vision went blurry all of a sudden
I see rainbow-colored rings around lights
My eye is red and I feel sick to my stomach

hpi.onset: Sudden, over minutes to a few hours, often in the evening or in a dark room
hpi.duration: Hours at presentation; pain is continuous until treated
hpi.progression: Rapidly worsening severe pain with declining vision; does not resolve on its own
hpi.location: One eye, often described as deep within or behind the eye
hpi.radiation: May spread to the forehead, temple, or cheek on the same side
hpi.quality: Deep, aching, boring pain that is constant
hpi.severity: Severe, often 8–10/10; frequently the worst eye pain the patient has ever had
hpi.timing: Constant, worse in dim light or at night
relieving: Nothing reliably helps; some relief with sitting upright or in bright light

associated_symptoms.text: Blurred vision in the affected eye
Seeing haloes or rainbow rings around lights

pertinent_negatives: Curtain or shade over part of the vision
Prior similar episodes that resolved on their own

argues_against: Floaters with flashes and a curtain over the vision (retinal detachment)
Contact lens use with a corneal infiltrate (keratitis)
Vomiting before the eye pain started (gastroenteritis)
Sinusitis with facial pain and purulent nasal discharge

atypical.how_it_differs: Pain may be milder or attributed to headache or dental pain, and vision loss may be noticed only after the episode; cataracts and multiple medications raise risk.
Rare; may present with irritability, vomiting, and refusal to open the eye rather than a clear description of pain or haloes.
Can be triggered by antiemetics with anticholinergic effects or by topiramate for migraine; symptoms may be mistaken for preeclampsia-related visual changes.

general.mild: Uncomfortable, holding the affected eye, but alert and not toxic
general.moderate: Distressed by pain, avoids bright light, may be nauseated
general.severe: Ill-appearing, writhing or holding the head, vomiting, unable to cooperate with a full exam
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, lethargic or confused from severe pain and vomiting

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to point to the pain and rate it
findings.finding: Severe deep eye pain, often 8–10/10, in one eye

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in natural light
findings.finding: Diffuse conjunctival and ciliary redness of the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Shine a light obliquely across the cornea and inspect clarity
findings.finding: Cloudy, steamy cornea that obscures the view of the iris

findings.maneuver: Shine a light into each eye and compare pupil size and reactivity
findings.finding: Mid-dilated pupil (4–6 mm) that does not react to light, often vertically oval

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity in each eye with a Snellen chart or pinhole
findings.finding: Reduced visual acuity in the affected eye, often markedly worse than the other eye

findings.maneuver: Shine a penlight from the temporal side at the level of the iris to assess the anterior chamber depth
findings.finding: Shallow anterior chamber with the iris appearing close to the cornea

findings.maneuver: Measure intraocular pressure with a tonometer (or estimate by digital palpation if unavailable)
findings.finding: Markedly raised intraocular pressure, typically 40–70 mm Hg

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with a slit lamp or penlight for epithelial microcysts and haze
findings.finding: Corneal epithelial edema with microcysts and loss of the normal light reflex

findings.maneuver: Inspect the perilimbal region for deep vessel injection
findings.finding: Ciliary flush (perilimbal injection) around the cornea

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to look at a bright light or shine a light near the eye
findings.finding: Pain or marked discomfort with light

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lower lid and cheek for tears
findings.finding: Excess tearing from the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lid margins and conjunctival sac for discharge
findings.finding: No purulent or mucoid eye discharge

findings.maneuver: Ask about new floaters or flashes and inspect the vitreous with a slit lamp if available
findings.finding: No new floaters or flashes of light

findings.maneuver: Test cranial nerves, strength, sensation, and coordination
Flex the neck and check for resistance or pain

findings.text: Corneal epithelial edema with microcysts obscuring the view of the iris
Shallow anterior chamber with a convex iris and iridocorneal touch
Closed or occluded iridocorneal angle on gonioscopy
Mid-dilated, vertically oval pupil that does not react to light
Markedly elevated intraocular pressure, typically 40–70 mm Hg

imaging.preferred_when: Corneal edema prevents a view of the posterior segment

findings.text: Normal posterior segment without retinal detachment or intraocular mass

initial.why: Confirms a closed angle and shows corneal edema and shallow anterior chamber

initial.only_if: the patient can cooperate and the cornea is clear enough

supporting.why: Evaluates the posterior segment when the cornea is too cloudy for a direct view
supporting.only_if: corneal edema prevents examination of the posterior segment

decision_points: Measure intraocular pressure and examine the angle before giving any pupil-dilating drops
Treat elevated intraocular pressure immediately; do not delay for additional testing
If corneal edema prevents gonioscopy, lower the pressure first and repeat the examination

differential.name: Acute anterior uveitis (iritis)
differential.why_considered: Painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision, the most common inflammatory red eye

history: Gradual onset over hours to days rather than minutes
Pain is aching and worse with eye movement, not deep and boring
No haloes around lights
Often associated with autoimmune disease or prior episodes
exam: Small or irregular pupil that may be constricted rather than mid-dilated and fixed
Ciliary flush with cells and flare in the anterior chamber on slit lamp
Keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium
Normal or only mildly elevated intraocular pressure
Deep anterior chamber with an open angle on gonioscopy
labs: No routine lab abnormality; testing directed at underlying systemic disease if suspected
imaging: Slit-lamp examination shows anterior chamber inflammation without a closed angle

differential.name: Acute bacterial conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Red, irritated eye with tearing and discomfort

history: Gritty or burning irritation rather than severe deep pain
Purulent or mucoid discharge with sticky lashes on waking
Vision is usually normal or only slightly blurry from discharge
No haloes, no nausea or vomiting
exam: Diffuse conjunctival injection that is worse peripherally and spares the perilimbal region
Normal pupil that reacts to light
Clear cornea without haze
Normal intraocular pressure
No anterior chamber inflammation
imaging: Slit-lamp examination shows no corneal edema and an open angle

differential.name: Corneal abrasion or infectious keratitis
differential.why_considered: Severe eye pain, tearing, photophobia and red eye with reduced vision
differential.trigger: Contact lens use, eye trauma, or a corneal epithelial defect that fluoresces with fluorescein

history: History of contact lens use, foreign body, or eye trauma
Pain is superficial and worse with blinking or a foreign body sensation
No haloes around lights
No nausea or vomiting
exam: Corneal epithelial defect or infiltrate that stains with fluorescein
Normal pupil that reacts to light
Normal or only mildly elevated intraocular pressure
Deep anterior chamber with an open angle
labs: Corneal scrapings for culture if a bacterial or fungal ulcer is suspected
imaging: Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein shows the epithelial defect without a closed angle

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless visual loss with flashes and floaters that can be mistaken for an acute eye problem
differential.trigger: New floaters with flashes of light and a curtain or shade over part of the vision

history: Painless visual loss
New floaters and flashes of light
Curtain or shade over part of the visual field
No deep eye pain, no haloes, no nausea
exam: Normal pupil reactivity unless the macula is involved
Normal intraocular pressure
Clear cornea without haze
Retinal tear or detachment seen on dilated fundoscopy
imaging: Ocular B-scan ultrasound shows a retinal detachment when the view is obscured

differential.name: Migraine with aura
differential.why_considered: Severe headache with visual disturbance and nausea or vomiting

history: Recurrent, stereotyped attacks over years
Visual symptoms are scintillating scotomas or zigzag lines that build up and resolve, not haloes around lights
Headache is throbbing and often bilateral
No red eye and no deep eye pain
exam: Normal eye examination with a white, non-injected eye
Normal pupil reactivity
Normal intraocular pressure
No corneal haze
imaging: Brain imaging is normal and not required for typical migraine

differential.name: Cluster headache
differential.why_considered: Severe unilateral periorbital pain with tearing and redness of the same eye

history: Attacks last 15 minutes to 3 hours and recur in clusters
Pain is strictly unilateral and centered on the orbit or temple
Restlessness and pacing during attacks
No haloes and no true visual loss
exam: Ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and eyelid edema (Horner syndrome)
Normal pupil reactivity to light
Normal intraocular pressure
Clear cornea without haze
imaging: Brain MRI is normal and used only to exclude secondary causes

differential.name: Scleritis
differential.why_considered: Severe, deep, boring eye pain with redness and photophobia

history: Gradual onset over days
Pain is severe and wakes the patient from sleep
Often associated with autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis
No haloes around lights
exam: Violaceous or deep scleral injection that does not blanch with phenylephrine
Tenderness of the globe on palpation
Normal pupil reactivity
Normal or mildly elevated intraocular pressure
Deep anterior chamber with an open angle
labs: Inflammatory markers and autoimmune serologies if an underlying systemic disease is suspected
imaging: Slit-lamp examination shows scleral thickening without a closed angle

severity.mild: Early or subacute angle closure: moderate eye pain, mild blurring, haloes only in dim light, intraocular pressure roughly 30–40 mm Hg, clear cornea, and no vomiting
severity.moderate: Established acute attack: severe deep eye pain, marked blurring, haloes, nausea, intraocular pressure roughly 40–55 mm Hg, corneal haze, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
severity.severe: Advanced acute attack: intense pain with vomiting, visual acuity reduced to counting fingers or worse, intraocular pressure above 55 mm Hg, dense corneal edema, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
severity.critical: Prolonged attack with threatened vision: intraocular pressure above 60 mm Hg with marked corneal edema, severe visual loss, and risk of permanent optic nerve damage; this is an ocular emergency rather than a systemic life threat

red_flags.meaning: Acute angle closure until proven otherwise; needs immediate pressure-lowering treatment

red_flags.finding: Fixed mid-dilated pupil with a cloudy cornea
red_flags.meaning: Classic acute angle-closure attack; do not give pupil-dilating drops

red_flags.finding: Severe eye pain with nausea and vomiting
red_flags.meaning: High risk of permanent optic nerve damage; treat as an emergency

red_flags.finding: Visual acuity reduced to counting fingers or worse
red_flags.meaning: Advanced optic nerve compromise; urgent ophthalmology involvement

red_flags.finding: Eye pain after starting topiramate or another triggering medication
red_flags.meaning: Drug-induced angle closure; stop the offending drug and treat the pressure

complications.name: Permanent optic nerve damage and visual field loss
clues: Persistent visual field defect after the pressure is lowered

complications.name: Iris atrophy and irregular pupil
clues: Irregular pupil that does not react normally after recovery

complications.name: Glaukomflecken (anterior lens opacities)
clues: Small white opacities under the anterior lens capsule after an acute attack

complications.name: Chronic angle-closure glaucoma with progressive vision loss
clues: Increasing cupping of the optic disc

complications.name: Recurrent acute attacks in the same or fellow eye
clues: Narrow angle in the fellow eye

Rare; may present with irritability, vomiting, and refusal to open the eye rather than a clear description of pain or haloes.
Can be triggered by antiemetics with anticholinergic effects or by topiramate for migraine; symptoms may be mistaken for preeclampsia-related visual changes.

key_questions.question: When did the eye pain start, and how fast did it come on?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over minutes to a few hours, often in the evening or in a dark room

key_questions.question: How severe is the pain, and where exactly do you feel it?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe deep, boring pain within or behind one eye, often the worst eye pain of their life

key_questions.question: Do you see haloes or rainbow-colored rings around lights?
key_questions.looking_for: Haloes around lights, a classic feature of acute angle closure

key_questions.question: Is your vision blurry or reduced in that eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Blurred or reduced vision in the affected eye

key_questions.question: Do you feel nauseated or have you vomited?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea and vomiting from severe pain; can be mistaken for a gastrointestinal illness

key_questions.question: Does the pain spread to your forehead, temple, or cheek?
key_questions.looking_for: Radiation to the forehead, temple, or cheek on the same side

key_questions.question: What were you doing when it started? Were you in a dark room or watching TV?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset in dim light or a dark environment, which dilates the pupil and precipitates the attack

key_questions.question: Have you had any eye trauma, eye surgery, or do you wear contact lenses?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; trauma or contact lens use points to corneal injury or keratitis instead

key_questions.question: Have you ever had an eye exam that showed a narrow angle or shallow anterior chamber?
key_questions.looking_for: Known narrow angle or shallow anterior chamber, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you recently had eye drops to dilate your pupils for an exam?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent pupil dilation, a common trigger

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medications such as topiramate, prednisone, ipratropium, oxybutynin, or amitriptyline?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticholinergic or sympathomimetic drugs that can precipitate angle closure

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have glaucoma or angle-closure glaucoma?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of angle-closure glaucoma in a first-degree relative

key_questions.question: Do you see new floaters, flashes of light, or a curtain or shade over part of your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; if present, consider retinal detachment instead

key_questions.question: Is there any discharge from the eye, or are your lashes sticky in the morning?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; purulent discharge suggests conjunctivitis or keratitis

key_questions.question: Have you had similar episodes before that went away on their own?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior self-limited episodes of blurring or haloes suggesting intermittent angle closure

reasoning_points: Sudden onset of severe unilateral deep eye pain over minutes to hours, often in dim light
Associated blurred vision and haloes around lights in the affected eye
Nausea and vomiting from severe pain, which can mimic a gastrointestinal illness
Red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a cloudy, steamy cornea
Markedly elevated intraocular pressure, typically 40–70 mm Hg
Shallow anterior chamber with a closed or occluded iridocorneal angle on gonioscopy
Risk factors such as age over 40, hyperopia, female sex, East Asian ancestry, and a family history of angle closure
Triggers such as pupil-dilating drops, dim environments, or anticholinergic and sympathomimetic medications
Retinal detachment, conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis, and migraine considered and excluded

easy: Older hyperopic woman with sudden severe unilateral eye pain
Classic haloes around lights and blurred vision
Red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and cloudy cornea
Markedly elevated intraocular pressure on tonometry
medium: Patient presents with nausea and vomiting and the eye symptoms are mentioned only on direct questioning
Pain radiates to the forehead or temple and is mistaken for migraine or sinusitis
Mild or subacute attack with moderate pain and only mild blurring
Triggered by recent pupil-dilating drops or a new anticholinergic medication
hard: Older adult with milder pain attributed to headache or dental pain and vision loss noticed only later
Patient taking topiramate for migraine with drug-induced angle closure
Corneal edema so dense that the iris and angle cannot be seen on initial examination
Pregnant patient with visual symptoms mistaken for preeclampsia-related changes
Younger patient without the typical age and sex pattern
